title: Cacio e Pepe
subtitle: Roman cheese and pepper pasta
excerpt: Three ingredients, one technique. The cheese must be grated to a near-powder to melt into the pasta water without clumping, and the pepper must be toasted first to bloom its oils. Nothing else is needed.
sourceNotes: Cacio e pepe is a Roman trattoria staple with roots in the cucina povera tradition, using only three ingredients. The name means cheese and pepper, and the dish relies entirely on technique to create a sauce from pasta water and cheese alone.

content.text: Use the finest grater setting you have for the parmesan -- coarse shreds will clump rather than emulsify. Toast the pepper in a dry pan before anything else so it is ready to go.

items.prepNote: very finely grated, plus extra to serve

content.text: Toast 2 teaspoons of coarsely ground black pepper in the dry frying pan over medium heat for 1-2 minutes until fragrant. Set aside.
Cook the spaghetti in well-salted boiling water. Reserve 200 ml of pasta water before draining.
Melt the butter in the frying pan over low heat. Add most of the toasted pepper and 80 ml of the reserved pasta water, stirring to combine.
Add the drained spaghetti to the pan and toss to coat. Remove from the heat.

Add the grated parmesan in two additions, tossing vigorously between each and adding pasta water a splash at a time until the cheese has melted into a creamy coating sauce. Serve with the remaining toasted pepper.

items.symptom: Cheese clumped into strings instead of a sauce.
items.cause: The pasta was too hot or the cheese was not fine enough.
items.fix: Let the pasta cool for 30 seconds off the heat before adding cheese, and always grate parmesan as finely as possible.
